frontmatter.title: Structural Inference Under Uncertainty: A Multimodal Synthesis

children.value: This chapter integrates the associations of a general worry factor with net placements, computational-model parameters, cursor movements, gaze, pupil size and self-reports. Every result is reported in detail in the chapters listed at the end. Each section below states one claim and the measures that bear on it. Effects are given as slopes per standard deviation (SD) of the questionnaire score; p-values refer to the models described in the linked chapters. All numbers are from run 23_11.

On each trial, participants place seven nets on 32 directions around a circle to block a mosquito attack. Attacks come from the direction of one of two hidden states (120° apart). The state switches at the start of each new episode (
), and within an episode, single attacks come from the direction of the other state (

). Two colour cues alternate across trials; each cue has its own pair of directions. Three instruction groups received no rules (None, n = 37), a mention that rules exist (Partial, n = 36), or a full explanation of the structure (Full, n = 22); these are the 95 participants with questionnaire scores. Eye-tracking and pupil measures are available for 84 to 87 of them (Full: 19 to 20).
are trials that are not transitions or oddballs and lie at least five trials after the last such event.
is the absolute angle between the centre of the nets and the direction of the current hidden state.

The five questionnaires (STICSA trait and state, BDI-II, OCI-12, IUS-12; 93 items) were submitted to a minimum-residual exploratory factor analysis with one group factor per questionnaire, and the general factor of the Schmid–Leiman transformation was extracted. The score of each participant is the sum of the z-scored item responses weighted by their general-factor loadings. The loadings used here were estimated in 83 online respondents without task data who passed all attention checks, and the task participants were scored with these loadings; this score correlates at r = .999 with the score whose loadings were estimated in all 178 respondents (

). The loadings are highest for the cognitive STICSA items, the OCI obsessing items and the inhibitory IUS items, so the factor weights worry-related content more than somatic anxiety. Because one factor score replaces the five scale scores, each measure is tested once. STICSA trait is reported alongside because it carries the largest single-scale effects.

Overall accuracy (all trials: −1.4° per SD of the general factor, p = .31), accuracy two trials after a transition (p = .96) and the learning rate on regular trials (+0.11 SD per SD, p = .20) are unrelated to the general factor. The scores are instead associated with

unexpected outcomes are used. After an attack from an unexpected direction, higher scorers keep their first net and their first fixation at the previously correct state, and two trials later they more often split their nets between the old and the new state. Meanwhile, cursor and gaze show that the alternative state is represented: the first cursor movement curves towards it, and gaze shifts between the two states correlate with the splitting. Once a second attack confirms a change, higher scorers move to the new state.

The instruction condition moderates the consequences of this pattern. With partial instructions, higher scores are associated with a smaller distance from the target on stable trials from the first episodes on, gaze that stays on the task-relevant directions, a larger pupil before the outcome, and a baseline pupil that covaries with the model’s state uncertainty and declines within each episode. With full instructions, these associations are absent or reversed in sign, and several of these slopes differ significantly from the partial-instruction slopes; in addition, higher scores are associated with longer placements before and after events, a stronger pupil response to surprise, higher noise reactivity in the model and a decrease of the rated aversiveness over the session. Without instructions, the scores are associated with the cursor trajectories, a larger pupil before the outcome and an increase of the rated aversiveness. Mean state valence is lower with higher scores in all conditions.

We interpret this pattern as follows. Higher scores are associated with interpreting single outcomes through an internal model of the task structure, so that an unexpected outcome is treated as noise until a further outcome confirms a change. Accordingly, when participants know that a structure exists but have to infer it (Partial), this tendency is associated with more accurate tracking of the hidden state. Conversely, when the structure is fully explained and only stochastic outcome noise remains (Full), higher scorers may attempt to account for every instructed possibility, which is consistent with longer placements, more fixations at the alternative state, stronger pupil responses to surprise and stronger attribution of outcomes to noise.

summarises the condition dependence. With partial instructions, higher general-factor scores are associated with more split placements at t+2 (+0.43 SD per SD, p = .026), a steeper decrease of the distance from the target after t+1 (−0.56, p = .010), a smaller distance on stable trials (−0.28, p = .037), less gaze beyond the task-relevant directions (−0.33, p = .003) and at the third direction (−0.26, p = .012), lower gaze entropy in the anticipation phase (−0.42, p = .030), a larger pupil before the outcome (+0.44, p = .038), a stronger coupling of the baseline pupil with the model’s state uncertainty (+0.40, p < .001) and a stronger decline of the baseline pupil within episodes (−0.46, p < .001). With full instructions, the slopes for the tracking, gaze and baseline-pupil measures are near zero or opposite in sign, whereas higher scores are associated with more split placements (+0.47, p = .010), longer placements on stable trials (+0.35, p = .045), higher noise reactivity (+0.38, p = .022) and a decrease of the rated aversiveness (−0.52, p = .001). The Full–Partial differences reach p < .05 for the baseline–uncertainty coupling (p = .012), the within-episode decline of the baseline pupil (p = .038) and the change in aversiveness (p = .035), and p < .10 for the decrease after t+1 (p = .054), the expected switch rate (p = .052) and the gaze beyond the task-relevant directions (p = .056). Without instructions, higher scores are associated with a larger pupil before the outcome (+0.34, p = .005) and an increase of the rated aversiveness (+0.31, p = .002).

1. After an unexpected attack, higher scorers keep their placement at the previously correct state

children.label: 1. After an unexpected attack, higher scorers keep their placement at the previously correct state

children.value: On the trial after a transition, the attack has come from the direction of the new state, but single attacks from that direction also occur on oddball trials. Several measures indicate that higher scorers do not yet treat this attack as a state change.

Higher general-factor scores are associated with following transitions less at t+1 (−0.21 log-odds per SD, p = .042). On the first trial of a new episode, the first net is placed at the direction of the previous state more often with higher STICSA trait (+0.40 log-odds per SD, p < .001) and IUS (+0.32, p = .018) (

In the anticipation phase, the first fixation falls on the direction of the believed current state more often with higher STICSA trait (+0.13 log-odds per SD, p < .001) and general factor (+0.10, p = .007). For STICSA trait, the slope is similar in the three conditions (+0.12, +0.14 and +0.13) and present in the first and the second half of the session (

In the variant of the latent-state model with an alternative action rule (lam), noise reactivity, which scales how strongly an outcome is attributed to the oddball component, is higher with the general factor (+0.19 SD per SD, p = .046) and with OCI (+0.27, p = .006). Within the conditions, this association is significant with full instructions (+0.38, p = .022) and not with partial instructions (+0.06, p = .78) or without instructions (+0.16, p = .38). In the adopted Nexus model, the expected switch rate h is lower with higher scores with partial instructions (−0.22 SD per SD, p = .17) and higher with full instructions (+0.24, p = .17; Full vs Partial p = .052).

In the model in which participants switch from a cue-wise tracker to a latent-state system, the weight on the latent-state system after the switch is lower with higher scores (−0.023 per SD, p < .001; participants with high reliance on the latent-state system), whereas the type of structure used (two coupled states vs four independent states) is unrelated to the general factor (p = .60). The lower weight comes mainly from participants without instructions (None −0.029 per SD, p < .001; Partial −0.015, p = .20; Full −0.022, p = .36; differences between the conditions p ≥ .31). It does not account for the split placements: the weight is unrelated to the share of split placements at t+2 in these participants (p = .85), and the general-factor slope on split placements does not decrease when the weight is added (+0.034 to +0.040 per SD). Higher scorers thus appear to use the same structure but to rely on it less fully, and this is separate from their splitting of the nets. The weight result depends on the four Nexus parameters of the latent-state system being free, which the model does not recover: with them fixed at the medians of the Nexus fits (variant hybrid7f), the weight is unrelated to the general factor (−0.008 per SD, p = .12; None −0.010, p = .45).

Attacks that carry no information about the state.

On trials with a net at the attack direction, the mosquito can still pass with a fixed probability. Such a bite therefore provides no information about the hidden state. After a bite on such a trial, compared with a blocked attack, the next placement moves towards the attack direction with partial instructions (+5.8°, p = .019), less without instructions (+3.6°, p = .19) and not with full instructions (−0.2°, p = .93; Full vs None and Partial p = .15). Higher IUS scores are associated with a smaller shift (−3.4° per SD, p = .031), most clearly without instructions (−4.9°, p = .050). In addition, the model surprise of these bites is lower with higher general-factor scores (−0.037 per SD, p = .021), mainly without instructions (−0.098, p < .001; None vs Partial p = .008, None vs Full p = .032): the fitted models of higher scorers expect such outcomes more. Two interpretations are compatible with these results: higher scores may go with less updating on outcomes that carry no information, or with a more accurate attribution of such outcomes to the stochasticity of the outcome.

2. The alternative state is represented while the placement stays at the believed state

children.label: 2. The alternative state is represented while the placement stays at the believed state

children.value: The placements described in section 1 could reflect a failure to register the alternative state. Several measures argue against this possibility.

At t+2 after a transition, higher scorers more often distribute their nets between the directions of the old and the new state (general factor +0.35 log-odds per SD, p = .009; STICSA state +0.33, BDI-II +0.33, OCI +0.31, STICSA trait +0.29, all p < .04; IUS +0.19, p = .21) (
). A split placement distributes the belief over both hypotheses.

Without instructions, the first cursor movement of a trial curves more towards the direction of the other state and changes direction more often with higher STICSA trait (curvature +0.13 per SD, p = .003; direction changes +0.09, p = .009; pull towards the other state +0.05, p = .005) (
). With partial or full instructions, these slopes are near zero; the first movement is instead pulled more towards the other state in all participants (Partial vs None p = .001).

Across participants, the frequency of gaze shifts between the two state directions during placement correlates with the frequency of split placements (ρ = .61). The share of gaze at the directions of the other colour cue increases more over the session with higher general-factor scores (+.023 per 100 trials and SD, p = .002).

In the anticipation phase, gaze returns to the direction of the most recent oddball attack more often than to a matched control direction (+2.5 percentage points of fixation time, p < .001). This difference is largest one trial after the oddball (+8.0 points), smaller two trials after it (+2.1 points) and absent from three trials on. Gaze also returns to the directions of the previous trial’s nets (+3.3 points, p < .001), more so with full instructions (+3.6 points, p = .007). These measures are unrelated to the general factor (all p ≥ .30); higher IUS scores are associated with less gaze at the last oddball location in the inter-stimulus interval (−1.1 points per SD, p = .035) (
Accuracy at t+2 is unrelated to the general factor (p = .96).

3. After a confirming attack, higher scorers move to the new state

children.label: 3. After a confirming attack, higher scorers move to the new state

children.value: With partial instructions, the larger distance of higher scorers at the transition and at t+1 is followed by a steeper decrease of the distance.

On the transition trial, whose placement was made before the new attack direction was observed, higher scorers are further from the direction of the new state (general factor +8.8° per SD, p = .011), because their nets are more concentrated at the direction of the old state. At t+1, the difference remains (+8.4°, p = .047).

From t+1 to the mean of t+2 to t+4, the distance decreases more with higher scores (general factor −13.7° per SD, p = .011; STICSA trait −13.0°, p = .007; STICSA state −12.3°, p < .001; difference between Partial and Full for the general factor: p = .054). In the median split of STICSA trait, high scorers are closer to the target at t+2 (−13.6°, p = .062) and t+3 (−11.0°, p = .093) (

High STICSA-trait scorers are also closer to the target one trial before the transition (−12.5°, p = .085). The smaller distance after confirmation is thus part of a more accurate tracking of the current state in general (section 4).

4. With partial instructions, higher scores are associated with more accurate state tracking

children.label: 4. With partial instructions, higher scores are associated with more accurate state tracking

children.value: With partial instructions, participants know that rules exist but have to infer them. In this condition, and only in this condition, higher scores are associated with better performance on several measures of state tracking.

Higher scorers are closer to the target on stable trials (general factor −6.1° per SD, p = .037; STICSA trait −7.6°, p = .004). The corresponding slopes are −1.1° (p = .74) without instructions and +0.2° (p = .95) with full instructions; the Partial and Full slopes differ for STICSA trait (p = .012) and not significantly for the general factor (p = .13) (

The association is present in episodes 1 to 4 (general factor −6.5°, p = .002; STICSA trait −7.4°, p < .001) and has a similar size in episodes 6 to 9 (general factor −6.5°, p = .18); its change over the session is unrelated to the scores (p = .99) (

). The information that rules exist may therefore suffice to elicit the association, without a gradual learning process. Consistently, the gaze associations with the scores are present in the first and the second half of the session.

The state uncertainty replayed from each participant’s fitted model on stable trials is lower with higher scores with partial instructions and higher with full instructions (STICSA trait: −0.035 and +0.033 per SD), but neither slope nor their difference is significant (Full vs Partial p = .13; general factor p = .24).

With partial instructions, higher scores are associated with a lower precision weighting in the lam variant (−0.145 per SD, p = .039; Nexus −0.115, p = .12). The precision weighting does not account for the smaller distance: a higher precision weighting is associated with a smaller distance, so that the score effect increases from −6.1° to −7.6° when the Nexus precision weighting is added to the model. The score effect decreases when the cue sensitivity (Nexus: to −3.9°) or the placement noise of the lam variant (to −3.8°) is added, but these parameters are unrelated to the score (p ≥ .11).

With partial instructions, higher scores are associated with less fixation time beyond the believed current state in the prediction phase (−0.33 SD per SD, p = .003; Full vs Partial p = .056), less fixation time at the third direction (p = .012), lower gaze entropy over the task-relevant directions in the anticipation phase (−0.111 bits per SD, p = .009) and in the outcome phase (−0.079 bits, p = .008), and more first fixations at the current and at the other state (current +0.154 log-odds, p = .030; other +0.155, p < .001). Gaze thus concentrates on the two state directions. Across conditions, higher scores are associated with less gaze at directions without nets (general factor −0.034, p = .016) and a longer lead of gaze over the cursor before the first net (+16 ms per SD, p = .049) (

In the inter-stimulus interval before the outcome, when the outcome cannot yet be known, the pupil is larger with higher scores with partial instructions (general factor +0.100 z per SD, p = .026) and without instructions (+0.078, p = .034), but not with full instructions (+0.038, p = .38) (

). The baseline pupil before each trial covaries with the model’s state uncertainty more strongly with higher scores with partial instructions (+0.039 per SD, p = .021; per participant r = +.43; Full vs Partial p = .007) (

). Within each episode, the baseline pupil of higher STICSA-trait scorers starts higher and declines faster (−0.077 z per 10 trials and SD, p = .003; Full vs Partial p = .020), so that it approaches the level of lower scorers towards the end of the episode (

). Across participants, a larger pupil response to surprise after the feedback is associated with a smaller distance on stable trials (r = −.52; Partial: r = −.59), and with partial instructions this response is larger with higher STICSA trait (r = +.45, p = .009) (

). Together, these results indicate that, with partial instructions, arousal in higher scorers is coupled to the model’s state uncertainty and decreases as the current state becomes established within an episode.

5. With full instructions, higher scores are associated with longer placements, stronger pupil responses to surprise and stronger attribution of outcomes to noise

children.label: 5. With full instructions, higher scores are associated with longer placements, stronger pupil responses to surprise and stronger attribution of outcomes to noise

children.value: With full instructions, participants know the two states, the oddballs, the switches and the colour cues; only the timing of switches and the occurrence of oddballs remain unpredictable. In this condition, higher scores are not associated with more accurate tracking. The following associations are observed instead.

Placements take longer with higher scores, both on stable trials (general factor +0.24 s per SD, p = .045) and on the trials after events (+0.26 s, p = .018). The slope is positive at every lag from two trials before to four trials after transitions and oddballs, and is similar for STICSA trait, OCI and BDI-II (
). Without or with partial instructions, the duration is unrelated to the scores. The additional time is not concentrated before the first net (+0.07 s, p = .37) or after it (+0.09 s, p = .27).

Noise reactivity in the lam variant is higher with the general factor (+0.38 SD per SD, p = .022). The feedback pupil covaries with the model’s oddball probability more strongly with full than with partial instructions (+0.104 vs +0.033, p = .026), and this coupling increases with the general factor in Full (+0.050 per SD, p = .041).

The feedback pupil scales with the surprise of the attack more strongly with higher general-factor scores (across conditions +0.042 per SD, p < .001; Full +0.060, p = .006; None +0.036, p = .040; Partial +0.036, p = .10) (
), and its scaling with the belief update increases with the score in Full (+0.040, p = .006; per participant r = +.48).
The baseline pupil does not decline within episodes with higher scores (STICSA trait p = .73) and does not covary with the model’s state uncertainty (r = −.32, p = .18).
Transfer to the other colour cue.

On the first trial with the other colour cue after a transition, the distance from the new target is larger with higher scores (STICSA trait: Full +11.1° per SD, p = .022; None +5.3°, p = .16; Partial +2.8°, p = .57). On the first trial with the colour cue of the transition, the distance is unrelated to the scores (p ≥ .08) (
). Higher scorers with full instructions therefore apply a change observed with one cue to the other cue later.

Higher scores are associated with more fixations at the other state when no net is placed there (general factor +0.36 log-odds per SD, p = .022; Full vs Partial p = .089), more gaze shifts between the two states (+0.47, p = .023; Full vs Partial p = .058) and more later nets at the other state (+0.71, p = .009; Full vs Partial p = .025).

The rated aversiveness increases less from the first to the second half of the session with higher scores (−18.0 points per SD, p = .001), whereas it increases more without instructions (+10.8, p = .002) and is unrelated to the scores with partial instructions (+1.2, p = .87; Full vs Partial p = .035) (

). Higher scorers report having noticed a rule slightly more often across conditions (+0.09 per SD, p = .046), but not within any condition (p ≥ .16); the clarity of the instructions is unrelated to the scores (p ≥ .18).

These associations are consistent with a larger set of hypotheses that higher scorers attempt to monitor when all rules are given: longer deliberation, more fixations at the alternative state, stronger pupil responses to surprise and stronger attribution of outcomes to the oddball component. Accordingly, the tendency that is associated with more accurate tracking under partial instructions is associated with longer deliberation and stronger responses to surprise under full instructions.

6. Pupil responses to surprise and the subsequent belief update

children.label: 6. Pupil responses to surprise and the subsequent belief update

children.value: Across conditions, the pupil after the feedback increases with the surprise of the attack (+0.081 z per SD of surprise) and with the size of the model’s belief update (+0.061), both p < .001. On the trial after a transition, the pupil during the attack animation is larger than on the trial after an oddball (+0.08 z, p = .006); the pupil thus differentiates a confirmed change from an isolated oddball. With higher scores, the relation between the pupil during the attack animation and the subsequent shift of the placement changes sign (general factor −1.64° per SD, p = .027): in lower scorers, a larger pupil precedes a larger shift, whereas in higher scorers a larger pupil precedes a smaller shift. Higher scorers therefore show a pupil response to the attack that is not followed by a corresponding update of the placement.

7. Associations shared by the three conditions

children.label: 7. Associations shared by the three conditions

children.value: Several gaze associations do not differ between the conditions and are present in both halves of the session. With higher STICSA trait, the first fixation in the anticipation phase falls on the current state more often (+0.13 log-odds per SD, p < .001), directions without nets are fixated less (−0.040, p = .002), the other state is fixated less when no net is placed there (−0.14, p = .026), gaze entropy over the task-relevant directions is lower in the anticipation phase (−0.055 bits, p = .030) and in the outcome phase (−0.045 bits, p = .020), and gaze precedes the cursor by a longer interval (gaze–cursor lag +22 ms per SD, p = .001). These associations describe a stable focus of gaze on the believed current state. The instruction condition determines whether this focus coincides with more accurate tracking (Partial) or not (None, Full).

Participants rated their state once per episode, after trial 7 or 14. Mean valence is lower with higher scores (general factor −5.6 points on the 0–100 scale per SD, p = .001; STICSA trait −4.4, p = .005). The association is present in each condition and largest with full instructions (general factor: None −4.5, p = .16; Partial −4.9, p = .12; Full −7.8, p = .014); the conditions do not differ significantly (Full vs Partial p = .51). Valence decreases over the episodes in all groups, and this decrease is unrelated to the scores (−0.12 points per SD and episode, p = .69) (

Within participants, valence covaries with tracking accuracy when the structure has to be inferred. After removing each participant’s linear trend over the episodes, valence is lower after episodes with a larger distance from the target with partial instructions (−1.3 points per SD of the distance, p = .009) and without instructions (−0.9, p = .068), but not with full instructions (+1.2, p = .098). With full instructions, valence tends to be lower after episodes with higher model-based state uncertainty (−1.2 points per SD, p = .12) (

). The general factor does not modulate the coupling of valence with the distance in any condition (p ≥ .15). With full instructions, more distributed gaze in the anticipation phase is associated with higher valence in lower but not in higher STICSA-trait scorers (score × gaze entropy −1.4, p = .030).

9. Results that do not fit the interpretation, and open questions

children.label: 9. Results that do not fit the interpretation, and open questions

children.value: The replayed state uncertainty is lower with higher scores under partial and higher under full instructions, but the difference is not significant (STICSA trait p = .13). The condition dependence therefore rests on tracking, gaze, pupil, placement duration and self-report, not on the model’s uncertainty.
The lower expected switch rate of higher scorers with partial instructions is not significant within the condition (p = .17); only the Full–Partial difference approaches significance (p = .052).

The pupil response to surprise is unrelated to the fitted noise reactivity (lam: r = −.10, p = .35). Instead, it is associated with a higher cue sensitivity (Nexus: r = +.35) and a lower placement noise (r = −.37). Higher scores go with a stronger, not a weaker, pupil response to surprise after the feedback (section 5), so the pupil gives no direct physiological correlate of attributing surprise to noise.
Pupil before the outcome with full instructions.
The pupil in the inter-stimulus interval does not covary more strongly with the model’s state uncertainty with higher scores under any condition (Partial −0.001, Full +0.004 per SD).
Transition vs oddball in the pupil.
The pupil difference between the trial after a transition and the trial after an oddball is unrelated to the scores in all conditions.

The fit advantage of the Nexus model over a simple tracking model is unrelated to the scores (p ≥ .12); the condition-dependent associations therefore do not reflect differences in which model describes the participants best.

Without instructions, higher scores are associated with a larger pupil before the outcome, a stronger pupil response to surprise, a lower model surprise of uninformative bites and an increase of the rated aversiveness over the session, but not with the distance from the target (p = .74). It is open whether these associations reflect the same tendency as in Partial without the information needed to turn it into more accurate tracking.

None of the fitted parameters accounts for the smaller distance of higher scorers with partial instructions; the cue sensitivity and the placement noise of the lam variant reduce the score effect but are themselves unrelated to the scores.

10. Implications for a multimodal account of structural inference in worry

children.label: 10. Implications for a multimodal account of structural inference in worry

children.value: The results support an account in which a transdiagnostic worry dimension relates to how evidence is interpreted rather than to overall accuracy or learning rate. Higher scorers register unexpected outcomes: the pupil responds to them, gaze returns to the location of the last oddball, and the cursor and the nets show that the alternative state is considered. Yet they interpret single unexpected outcomes through an internal model of the task structure and change their placement only after a second outcome confirms a change. Accordingly, whether this tendency is associated with better or worse performance depends on the information available. With partial instructions, the structure has to be inferred, and higher scores are associated with more accurate tracking, gaze concentrated on the two states, an arousal level that is coupled to the model’s state uncertainty and decreases within each episode, and a valence that covaries with tracking accuracy. With full instructions, only stochastic outcome noise remains to be explained, and higher scores are associated with longer deliberation, more fixations at the alternative state, stronger pupil responses to surprise, stronger attribution of outcomes to noise and a decrease of the rated aversiveness over the session.

Three implications follow for computational psychiatry. First, symptom dimensions may be described more precisely by how evidence for a change is weighed against an internal model than by a general tendency to update more or less. Second, the sign of an association between a symptom dimension and task performance can depend on the information provided about the task structure; tasks with and without explicit structure can therefore yield opposite associations in the same population. Third, distributional responses (seven nets) and continuous process measures (cursor, gaze, pupil) are required to detect this pattern: a single point estimate per trial would not reveal split placements, and without process measures the represented alternative and the within-episode decline of arousal would not be observable.
